questions.q: Describe the erosional and depositional landforms produced by running water.
answer: Running water is the most important agent shaping the land, and it produces both erosional and depositional landforms.

answer.text: In its upper course, where the slope is steep, a river cuts down vigorously to form deep V-shaped valleys, gorges and canyons. Where hard and soft rocks alternate, waterfalls develop, and swirling water drills potholes into the river bed. In the middle course the river swings from side to side, carving looping bends called meanders.

As the river slows on gentler slopes it drops its load. At the foot of hills it builds alluvial fans, and along its lower course it lays down wide floodplains and raised banks called natural levees. A meander may be cut off to form an ox-bow lake, and at the mouth the river deposits a fertile delta.

answer: Thus a single river both carves and builds landforms along its course.

questions.q: How do glaciers shape the landscape through erosion and deposition?

answer.text: are moving masses of ice that carve and reshape the land as they flow slowly downhill.

list: They carve U-shaped valleys, bowl-shaped hollows (cirques) and sharp peaks (horns) in mountains
They pluck and grind rock as they move

answer.text: they leave material behind as they melt.

list: They dump unsorted rock and debris as ridges called moraines
Melting glaciers spread out sand and gravel as outwash plains, giving glaciated regions their special scenery

questions.q: How does wind shape landforms in desert regions?

answer.text: where there is little water or vegetation, the wind becomes the chief agent shaping the land.

list: Wind carrying sand blasts and polishes rocks, carving mushroom-shaped rocks and hollows
It sweeps away loose sand, leaving stony surfaces
When the wind slows, it drops sand to form dunes of various shapes, such as crescent-shaped barchans
Fine dust carried far and deposited forms fertile loess plains
